title: Ultrasensitive photodetectors enabled by pressure-induced atomic-level optimization of graphene-based heterojunctions

paper_content.abstract:
Photodetectors with high photoresponsivity are crucial in a wide range of emerging fields.
Here, we report the realization of photodetectors based on co-assembled composite
membranes consisting of copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) molecules and graphene oxide (GO)
sheets, showing a photoresponsivity as high as ~10⁷ A/W under 3 nW illumination and a
moderate external pressure (~1 atm) in the visible range. We attribute the high
photoresponsivity to the pressure-induced optimization of the atomic-level heterojunctions
between photoactive CuPc molecules and adjacent GO sheets in the photodetector, which
enhances the electronic coupling at the heterojunction for charge transport. The
photodetectors show good flexibility for electronic skin applications, enabling simultaneous
contact sensing and non-contact perception under ambient illumination down to dim
moonlight. The developed strategy provides a promising perspective for fabricating next-
generation photoelectric conversion devices with potential applications spanning intelligent
sensing, aerospace technologies, and defence-related photonic platforms.
paper_content.introduction:
Photodetectors that convert light into electrical signals are essential for diverse advancing
technologies, such as living cell and biomedical imaging, optical communication, night vision, and
security systems1-5. High photoresponsivity (the responsivity of the photodetector), i.e., the ratio
of the net photocurrent to the incident-light power, is of great importance in practical applications.
Intensive efforts and significant achievements have been made6-16; however, there is only little
progress on the raising of photoresponsivity under the common range of illumination powers (3
nW ‒ 10 mW) in the past decade (Fig. 1d), thus calling for new innovative strategy.

In optoelectronic devices, particularly those based on organics, photoactive materials absorb light
to produce excitons (coupled electrons and holes), and the electrons/holes resulting from the
dissociated excitons transport to the respective acceptor material through a heterojunction17-20. The
performance of the heterojunction is crucial for the photoresponsivity21-24. However, unfavourable
factors, such as defects and unevenness in the photoactive and/or acceptor materials, can degrade
the electronic coupling at the heterojunction for charge separation and transport16,25-27. Clearly,
these unfavourable factors are at the atomic/molecular level, making it very challenging to reduce
the detrimental effects. Fortunately, for materials with a planar architecture, a macroscopic
manipulation (i.e., applying an external pressure) can drive atomic/molecular-level modifications.
Based on our previous works on graphene oxide (GO)28-30, we recently fabricated a composite
membrane consisting of planar structures of copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) molecules and GO
sheets, where CuPc and GO serve as typical photoactive and electron-acceptor materials,
respectively31. We expected that a simple macroscopic manipulation could reduce some
detrimental effects to make a more compact CuPc‒GO heterojunction, thus leading to an even
higher photoresponsivity.

Electronic skins (e-skins) hold great transformative potentials32,33. Current e-skin technologies
predominantly rely on contact-based sensing modalities to acquire environmental information34,35.
Although this mode is effective for static scenarios, it fails to address dynamic environments
requiring non-contact interactions, such as robot-assisted navigation or preemptive hazard
detection in vehicular safety systems. Conventional optical e-skins, employing radar, laser, or
infrared light, require additional active illumination, and face critical limitations under passive
natural light conditions36. Clearly, if there is an ultrasensitive photodetector to detect direction and
distance, as well as flexibility and piezoelectricity to monitor the subjected pressure, we can obtain
a dual-mode e-skin simultaneously realizing contact and non-contact sensing under ambient
illumination.

Here, we present a photodetector based on a co-assembled composite membrane consisting of
CuPc molecules and GO sheets (CuPc@GO), exhibiting high responsivity under 3 nW ‒ 10 mW
incident powers and moderate external pressure within the near-ultraviolet, visible and infrared
bands. We associate the high photoresponsivity to the optimization of the atomic-level CuPc‒GO
heterojunctions via a macroscopic manipulation ‒ by simply applying a modest external pressure
(~1 atm), a strong electronic coupling at the heterojunction is established and a ~105 to 106-fold
improvement in photoresponsivity is obtained. The photodetector is successfully used in dual-
mode e-skins, enabling flexibility together with simultaneous contact and non-contact sensing,
within the irradiation range from daylight to moonlight.
paper_content.results:
High photoresponsivity obtained under external pressure

The central component of the photodetector is a CuPc@GO membrane fabricated via a drop
casting method. Briefly, a CuPc suspension was mixed with a GO dispersion. The mixture was
then dripped onto release paper and dried, yielding a composite membrane. The membrane was
subsequently employed to fabricate a CuPc@GO photodetector.

To ensure that the embedded CuPc molecules contact the GO sheets well, we applied an external
force (i.e., pressure) on the CuPc@GO membrane. Henceforth, we refer to the CuPc@GO
membranes with and without the pressure as optimized and unoptimized membranes, respectively.
Simultaneously, we illuminated the optimized CuPc@GO membrane with a beam of light on the
opposite side from the pressure application site, with the illuminated area of 1 cm2 identical to the
area under external pressure (Fig. 1a). In this paper, the illumination wavelength is 635 nm (visible
light) unless otherwise explicitly stated. The current‒voltage (I‒V) performance with an incident
power E = 3 nW was examined firstly (Fig. 1b). As the bias ranges from -1.2 to 1.2 V, the
in
photocurrent increases with the increasing pressure (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1). When the
external pressure (denoted as P) reaches 240 kPa, the photocurrent increases to 4.41 × 10-2 A under
a bias of 1.2 V, in contrast to the dark current of 4.11 × 10-3 A. Notably, the photocurrent and dark
current in the unoptimized case are only 5.35 × 10-8 A and 1.87 × 10-8 A, respectively. Thus, the
light response is boosted by more than 105 times under P = 240 kPa, while it is only modest in the
absence of the external pressure.

The high photoresponsivity shows strong stability (Supplementary Figs. 6&7) and reproducibility

Characterization of CuPc@GO membrane under pressure

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern (Fig. 2a) indicates an intersheet spacing of 0.826 nm for the
unoptimized CuPc@GO membrane, which is slightly larger than that for the pure GO membrane
(0.731 nm). This suggests that the CuPc molecules, which have a planar structure and single-atom
thickness, intercalate into the GO membrane and form a single-molecule layer sandwiched
between two adjacent GO sheets. The intercalation of CuPc is also supported by scanning electron
microscopy (SEM), where a well-defined layered structure (Fig. 2b) of the CuPc@GO membrane
(unoptimized) was clearly revealed. Compared with the pure GO membrane, a new sharp
diffraction peak in the XRD pattern (Fig. 2a) appears at ~26° for the CuPc@GO membrane,
corresponding to an interplanar spacing of ~0.334 nm, indicating the stacking of CuPc aromatic
rings with the unoxidized regions40,41 of the GO sheets.

The XRD patterns after the pressure application are shown in Fig. 2a. Notably, as the pressure
increases, the intersheet spacing of the composite membrane decreases continuously (Fig. 2c), and
the peak at ~26° corresponding to an interplanar spacing of 0.334 nm becomes more apparent.
These phenomena indicate that the confined space between the GO sheets is gradually regulated
such that more π‒π stacks are enabled between the aromatic rings of the CuPc molecules and the
GO sheets.

We further performed femtosecond transient absorption (TA)42 spectroscopy measurements (with
an external pressure ~25 kPa; see Methods). The TA spectra of the optimized (Fig. 2d) and
unoptimized (Supplementary Fig. 12) membranes pumped by a 400 nm laser pulse show clear
excited-state absorbance (ESA) signals peaking at ~650 nm, whereas ground-state bleaching (GSB)
and stimulated emission (SE) signals are not observed. The ESA signals span a broad range of
wavelengths, from ~550 nm to 800 nm (and beyond), and exhibit a large overlap with the typical
absorption spectrum of the CuPc molecule (Supplementary Fig. 13), indicating that the
photocurrent is mainly caused by the optical absorption of CuPc molecules. The absence of GSB
and SE signals can be attributed to aggregation-induced quenching43 of excitons in CuPc molecules
because of their strong π‒π stacking with neighbouring GO sheets, which leads to ultrafast charge
dynamics and is beneficial to the high photoresponsivity.

Mechanism of the pressure-enhanced photoresponsivity

To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we performed density functional theory (DFT)
calculations on the unit cell of the composite membrane ‒ a sandwich complex where one CuPc
molecule is placed between adjacent GO sheets. Here we used a simplified GO model44: one
epoxide group and one hydroxy group were located closely to each other and separately on both
sides of the GO sheet, leaving a relatively large region unoxidized. This model is consistent with
previous reports that the oxidized groups tend to gather and there are large unoxidized regions on
the GO sheets40,41. Considering the observation of remarkable π‒π stacking interactions between
the CuPc molecules and the GO sheets (Fig. 2b,c), the CuPc molecule was placed in the middle of
the unoxidized regions of the GO sheets. Two typical states were considered: the coupling state
and the uncoupling state, corresponding to the cases of small and large intersheet distance,
respectively (see Fig. 3a,b). In the coupling state, a CuPc molecule has an equal distance of 0.327
nm with each GO sheet, yielding the intersheet distance of 0.654 nm according to structural
optimization (Fig. 3a). The coupling state corresponds to the pressure-optimized configuration.

The well-dispersed valence and conduction bands (Fig. 3c) and the delocalized electronic
wavefunction distribution (Fig. 3a) clearly indicate strong electronic coupling at the CuPc‒GO
interface. Consequently, a charge-transport channel is well formed perpendicular to the GO sheets,
which is bridged by the CuPc molecule. The valence and conduction bandwidths are 13.8 meV
and 8.2 meV, respectively, which corresponds to a coupling at the CuPc‒GO interface of 3.5 meV
for the hole and 2.1 meV for the electron according to the one-dimensional tight-binding model.
This result is consistent with our ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) data, which show
a shift in the valence band position due to pressure optimization (Supplementary Fig. 14). In
addition, we calculated the intra-sheet and inter-sheet electric conductivities to quantitively
characterize the relative contributions of intra- and inter-sheets to charge transport as well as the
influence of pressure (see Supplementary Fig. 15). The inter-sheet conductivity is still lower than
the intra-sheet conductivity even after the optimization, indicating that the inter-sheet transport
still represents the main bottleneck limiting charge transport in the overall GO‒CuPc‒GO pathway.

In the typical uncoupling state, the intersheet distance was set to be 0.826 nm, corresponding to
the intersheet spacing of the unoptimized CuPc@GO membrane (see Fig. 2b). The valence and
conduction bandwidths are sharply reduced to 0.9 meV and 1.6 meV, respectively. We also show
the case of pure GO system (parallel GO sheets without CuPc) as the control group in Fig. 3c,
where the bandwidths are also negligible due to the absence of intersheet interactions. These results
indicate negligible electronic coupling in the uncoupling case, as also demonstrated by the much
more localized electronic wavefunction distribution along the perpendicular direction (Fig. 3b).
Now we can illustrate how efficient charge-transport pathways are established in the CuPc@GO
membrane and why the applied pressure serves as a key. As shown in Fig. 3d, the CuPc molecules
are distributed between the GO sheets. There are two processes associated with the transport of
charge carriers: (i) the electron transfer from the CuPc molecule onto the neighbouring GO sheet
due to exciton dissociation; and (ii) the intra-sheet and inter-sheet (via a GO‒CuPc‒GO pathway)
charge transport. In the absence of the external pressure, due to the relatively large distance
between CuPc and GO sheets, there are rare coupling states to form efficient pathways for charge
transfer and intersheet charge transport (Fig. 3e). However, through the application of pressure,
most hindrance mentioned above are removed and much more coupling states with efficient
charge-transport pathways are well established (Fig. 3d), thus resulting in a high photocurrent.

Dual-mode-sensing electronic skin of the photodetector

We fabricated a CuPc@GO-based electronic skin (CuPc@GO e-skin) which can work in both non-
contact and contact sensing modes (Fig. 4a). We note that the CuPc@GO photodetector has good
flexibility with high photoresponsivity remaining at various bending/twisting angles (Fig. 4b and
Supplementary Figs. A16&17). Thus, the photodetector can have more applications requiring
flexibility45 such as the e-skin. Standard models with sizes of ~10 cm were used to testify the dual-
mode sensing under ambient illumination with E = 10 μW, corresponding to the ambient
in
illumination just at dawn (~9.5 lux for the CuPc@GO membrane with an area of 1 × 1 cm2). As e-
skin approaches the models, the photocurrents decrease commenced at the distances of 15 mm, 12
mm, and 5 mm, for cuboid, hemisphere and stick, respectively, exhibiting dependence on both
object geometry and separation distance (Fig. 4c). Once the e-skin contacts the models, an abrupt
current increase is observed (Fig. 4c), which also exhibits a shape-dependent manner mainly due
to the piezoelectricity of the CuPc@GO membrane (see Ref. 31 and Supplementary Table 2). The
e-skin can also distinguish the hardness of objects ‒ an object with higher hardness can induce a
more abrupt current increase as the e-skin contacts the object (Fig. 4d). As the target size increases,
the e-skin shows an extended range of object discrimination, enabling non-contact detection at
distances up to 2 m for the target with a size of ~1 m (Fig. 4e). Remarkably, the e-skin can “see”
the object even under a power of 900 pW (Fig. 4f), corresponding to the ambient illumination
under the moonlight (~0.01 Lux for the CuPc@GO membrane).

We designed a control board for signal acquisition and actuation of the robotic manipulator (Fig.
4g and Supplementary Fig. 18), which was subsequently installed on a robotic manipulator
incorporating the CuPc@GO e-skin into the fingertips (Fig. 4h). A series of actions including
approaching, grasping, moving and releasing were conducted by using the robotic manipulator
according to the e-skin feedback, and the featured responses in the photocurrent are explicated in
Fig. 4i, with the middle fingertip as a typical example to illustrate the idea (Fig. 4j). Firstly, the
middle finger was controlled to approach the target object, inducing a decreasing photocurrent.
According to the results of standard models, a 1.9% reduction in the photocurrent serves as a
threshold for impending mechanical contact. Once the current decreased lower than this threshold,
the approaching velocity was initially halved and then progressively attenuated to 0.9 mm/s,
thereby minimizing impulse transfer to the object. The manipulating examples with a banana (Fig.
4i,j) and an egg (Supplementary Fig. 19) the successfully touching on the objects while avoiding
damage. During the releasing process, all fingers retract simultaneously, exhibiting fast decreases
in the current (Fig. 4i,j and Supplementary Fig. 19).
paper_content.methods:
Materials

The Copper phthalocyanine and Graphite were provided by Aladdin Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China)
with a purity beyond 99.95%. Potassium persulfate (K S O ), Phosphorus pentoxide (P O ),
2 2 8 2 5
Sulfuric acid (H SO ), Potassium permanganate (KMnO ) and Hydrogen peroxide (H O ) were
2 4 4 2 2
purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. All reagents were used as received. Milli-
Q water (18.25 MΩ, Millipore, US) was used to prepare GO aqueous dispersions. The
programmable robotic manipulator (uHand 2.0) was provided by Hiwonder Tech Co., Ltd.
(Shenzhen, China).

Preparation of CuPc@GO composite membranes and photodetectors

A GO suspension (5 mg/mL) was prepared with GO synthesized from natural graphite powder
using an improved Hummers method. A CuPc suspension was prepared by adding 28.68 mg of
powder to a centrifuge tube containing 50 mL of water, followed by an ultrasonic treatment for 1
hour. The CuPc dispersion was thoroughly mixed with the 5 mg/mL GO dispersion in equal
volumes. Ultrapure water of the same volume was subsequently added, and the resulting mixture
was processed with ultrasonic treatment for 1 hour to yield a stable CuPc@GO suspension. The
composite suspension was then divided into equal-volume droplets, which were dripped onto
release paper for self-assembly and dried in an oven at 70℃ for 12 hours. This process resulted in
the formation of the CuPc@GO composite membrane which has a thickness of ~1 μm with good
flexibility. Next, the membrane was peeled off from the release paper and then trimmed into square
pieces measuring 1 × 1 cm2. The CuPc@GO membrane within this photodetector served as the
photon-sensing layer.

Measurement of the photodetector properties

The I‒V characteristics and photocurrent versus time curves of the photodetectors were measured
using a Keithley 2461 source meter (Tektronix, USA) following rigorous experimental procedures.
To ensure accurate signal transmission and to minimize external interference, a gold probe was
employed during the photocurrent measurements. The external pressure was applied by the weight
unless otherwise explicated stated and was calibrated with commercial pressure transducers. The
incident light sources were monochromatic lasers (Thorlabs, USA) with an adjustable power
density and were precisely calibrated with photodiode power detectors (Thorlabs, S170C and
PM100D, USA) with 10 nW detection limit. The 3-nW incident power was achieved by attenuating
the 10 nW source through a neutral density filter with 30% transmittance. The illumination position
and area (1 cm2) were kept consistent throughout all the measurements, except for the case of 100
pW incident power which was achieved by reducing the effective optical area of the device to 0.1
× 0.1 cm² via a mask. Notably, no light source other than the laser was present in the measured
environment. Moreover, the photodetectors were tested under conditions consisting of room
temperature (25°C), 20% humidity, and atmospheric pressure. The rise and decay times were
obtained using an oscilloscope (Tektronix, MSO44 4-BW-200).

Characterization of the CuPc@GO membranes

Lateral images of the CuPc@GO membranes were acquired via secondary electron imaging in the
scanning electron microscope (ZEISS Gemini 300, Germany) at an accelerating voltage of 3 kV.
Patterns of X-ray diffraction were obtained via XRD (Rigaku Ultimate IV, Japan) with a Cu Kα
radiation source (λ = 0.15418 nm) in the 2θ range of 5°~40°. Before the XRD experiments were
conducted, pressures with different values (ranging from 20 to 240 kPa) were applied to the
CuPc@GO membrane for 5 minutes. There is no pressure applied on the sample during the XRD
experiments.

Transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy

Femtosecond TA spectroscopy was carried out using a Helios ultrafast pump‒probe system, which
included an oscillator and a Coherent Opera Solo optical parametric amplifier. The titanium
sapphire amplifier in the system generates 800 nm pulses at a repetition rate of 1 kHz, with each
pulse having a duration of 70 fs. These pulses are split by a beam splitter: one portion is directed
to a TOPAS parametric amplifier (Coherent) to produce the pump pulses while the other is focused
onto sapphire and YAG plates, generating a white supercontinuum that covers the 420–780 nm and
800–1400 nm ranges, respectively. The time delay between the pump and probe pulses has a
maximum value of 8 ns when a motorized optical delay line is used.

In order to meet the requirements of the TA spectroscopy measurement, both the membrane
thickness and the pressure applied are different from those of other experiments: i) the TA
measurement requires the sample surface to be very flat, so the CuPc@GO suspension was
carefully deposited via the drop-casting technique onto a 2 cm × 2 cm high-clarity quartz glass
substrate, followed by drying in an oven at 70°C. This results in a membrane thickness of ~ 100
nm, much thinner than that in other experiments (~1 μm). ii) Considering the fragility of the glass,
we applied a small pressure of ~25 kPa on the sample for 5 minutes. During the TA spectroscopy
measurements, the pressure was removed.

Dual-mode sensing of the electronic skin

The flexible CuPc@GO photodetector was mounted at the fingertip of a robotic manipulator to
maintain its optimal operational state during photodetection. For non-contact sensing, the robotic
system drove the fingertip in a programmed, controlled trajectory, advancing it toward the target
object until the initial surface contact was established. After contact, the system applied a
controlled compressive force by advancing the fingertip an additional 1 mm. During the entire
process, the current signals were monitored in real-time. Dynamic analysis on the current variation
enables the real-time capture of the mechanical interaction state between the fingertip and the
object, facilitating closed-loop feedback for precise adjustment of the motion trajectory of the
manipulator. This adaptive strategy ensures both accuracy and efficiency in the process of object
grasping. Environmental illumination remained stable throughout all experimental procedures.

Theoretical calculations

DFT calculations were performed with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)46.
Projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials were applied. The generalized gradient
approximation (GGA) of the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) formalism was used to treat the
exchange‒correlation interaction between electrons47, and the DFT-D3 method of Grimme with a
zero-damping function48 was applied for dispersion correction. The electron wavefunction was
expanded on a plane-wave basis set with an energy cutoff of 450 eV. The Brillouin zones were
sampled by k-point grids of 2 × 2 × 3 for structural optimization49.

For structural optimization of the state without an external pressure, the periodicity along the
direction perpendicular to the GO sheets was set to 0.826 nm, consistent with the XRD result,
whereas those along the other two directions were calculated to fully relax the stress. To describe
the state with an external pressure, the restriction of the periodicity along the z-axis was released,
and the structure was reoptimized via DFT calculations, resulting in a new periodicity of 0.654 nm,
which represents the deformation influenced by the external pressure. After the entire structural
optimization process, the number of k-points in the Brillouin zone was increased, and non-self-
consistent calculations were performed to obtain the energy band. By using the one-dimensional
tight-binding model, the intersheet electronic coupling 𝑡 for electrons/holes was then

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors reported the fabrication of the photodetectors based on copper phthalocyanine/graphene oxide heterojunctions and investigated their photoelectrical properties. They found that high photoresponsivity can be achieved by enhancing electronic coupling between photoactive copper phthalocyanine molecules and adjacent graphene oxide sheets through pressure. The further demonstrated dual-mode electronic skin application, operable under illumination ranging from daylight to moonlight. Their study is interesting and useful, supported by rigorous experimental validation, theoretical modeling, and practical demonstrations. I recommend acceptance pending revisions to s to address the following technical and conceptual aspects:
1. While the drop-casting method is simple, its reproducibility over larger areas and feasibility for industrial-scale production should be discussed, along with potential challenges in uniformity and yield.
2.Address the long-term stability of the pressure-optimized heterojunctions under cyclic mechanical stress (beyond Supplementary Fig. 6).
3.Elaborate on how this strategy (pressure-optimized heterojunctions) could be generalized to other optoelectronic systems (e.g., perovskites or 2D materials).
4.Discuss potential limitations (e.g., sensitivity to humidity or oxidation of GO) and mitigation strategies.
5.Clarify whether the 100 pW detection limit (Fig. 1f) requires cryogenic conditions or is achievable at room temperature.
6. Given graphene’s inherent high conductivity, additional experimental or theoretical evidence quantifying the relative contributions of intra-sheet versus inter-sheet (GO‒CuPC‒GO pathway) electron transport would further solidify the proposed mechanism.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors proposed a photodetector based on the CuPC/GO heterojunction using the vertical device structure. The device demonstrated significant responsivity enhancement after applying external forces. This work lacks sufficient innovation and the conclusions need additional data for support. I do not think it is suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
1. The main novelty of this paper is the use of external pressure to enhance device performance. However, applying pressure to improve the contact and reduce the interlayer distance in layered materials is a known and expected phenomenon. Furthermore, this work did not address the key concerns regarding the reproducibility of the method and the device-to-device variation under pressure. The authors show that the performance of one device is enhanced by more than 10^5 times when a pressure of 240 kPa is applied, but they don't provide data to show whether other devices would require the same pressure to achieve a similar performance improvement and whether this improvement could be controlled or repeated under multiple pressure-release cycles. The absence of these data makes the approach for performance enhancement is not a fundamentally new and reliable principle. I think the novelty of using external pressure is not solid.
2. Some basic and crucial performance characterizations are missing. For example, there are no results about the detectivity, LDR, or frequency response of the device, which are essential for evaluating a photodetector's performance. As a flexible device, the mechanical stability, including performance under repeated bending and complex strain, is not fully explored. Furthermore, the authors claim that the piezoelectricity of the CuPC@GO membrane is the reason for the abrupt current increase during contact sensing in Fig. 4c, however, there is no characterization about the piezoelectricity in this work. And I did not find any works reporting about the piezoelectricity of the CuPc and GO.
3. In the DFT calculation, the authors used pristine graphene instead of GO due to that GO sheets have "large unoxidized regions" and "remarkable π-π stacking interactions". However, this is a significant simplification that ignores the effects of oxygen-containing functional groups in GO, which could act as charge trapping sites. The authors should provide a clear explanation for the use of pristine graphene.
4. The authors claimed that the photodetector outperforms all current state-of-the-art devices under illumination powers from 3 nW to 10 mW. However, some published works have reported a higher photoresponsivity (Nat Commun 2021, 12, 1798). A more comprehensive and up-to-date literature review should be provided.
5. The paper's organization could be improved to enhance the readability. The current figure sequence is confusing. For example, Fig. 1d was cited as the first figure in the main text. The Fig. 2d and 2e appeared after the Figure 3. The illumination intensity with unit of nm/cm2 of μW/cm2 is more common for the comparison of responsivity while also providing the applied voltages.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this article, the authors claim to propose a dual-mode electronic skin (e-skin) based on the CuPc@GO photodetector. However, there are numerous loopholes:
1) In the experimental part, important information about the protocols used is missing. Common parameters for photodetectors, such as specific detectivity (D*), response bandwidth fc, the optical effective area Ad and noise equivalent power (NEP) must be thoroughly characterized. The authors have only presented data on responsivity and response time, which is insufficient to support the claimed potential for future applications. I believe this literature would be highly beneficial for the authors to deepen their understanding of photodetectors. (Wang, F., Zhang, T., Xie, R. et al. How to characterize the figures of merit of two-dimensional photodetectors. Nat. Commun. 14, 2224 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37635-1.)
a) The photoelectric properties shown in Fig.1 are difficult to regard as those of the CuPc@GO because they strongly reflect the properties of CuPc. It is recommended to make and measure the lateral device, using CuPc or GO.
b) In Fig. 1b, what is the mechanism behind the phenomenon where the device exhibits current at 0V without applied pressure, but this current disappears after pressure is applied?
c) In Fig. 1c, how did the authors manage to detect light as weak as 3 nW, which is notoriously difficult to measure with conventional power meters?
d) In Fig. 1d, why does the photoresponsivity reported in the latest literature appear lower than in earlier studies? Has the performance in this field been deteriorating?
e) In Fig. 1f, it is highly unusual that the device exhibits current at the milliampere level alongside significant noise under illumination as low as 100 pW. The authors must provide a plausible explanation for this anomalous data.
f) In Fig. 1g, when calculating the photoresponse time, it is advisable to normalize the data to clearly illustrate the range from 10% to 90% of the photocurrent variation.
2) Basic characterization experiments were conducted, but some results lack clarity, making analyzing the material's electrical performance less robust.
a) As a photoactive material, providing the ultraviolet absorption spectrum, UPS data, and energy band diagram of CuPc@GO is essential. Unusually, the experimental work utilizes GO, while the simulations are based on graphene. Such limited computational modeling is unconvincing. Synchrotron radiation experiments are necessary to characterize the bonding and carrier distribution in the heterojunction material.
b) Schematic of the network-like pathways of electron transport in fig. 3d-e is confusing; the electrical conductivity of graphene oxide is relatively poor. What role does graphene oxide play in the process of carrier separation? Furthermore, when asymmetric electrodes with significant potential barriers are employed, it is crucial to determine whether the photocurrent generation originates from the material itself or from the Schottky barrier at the electrode interface. Comparative experiments are necessary to clarify this mechanism.
3) For applications in flexible electronic skin, comprehensive characterization of mechanical properties is essential. The authors merely conducted simple tests at different bending angles, which is far from sufficient. It is necessary to evaluate the maximum number of bending cycles at various angles and quantify the variance in photoresponsivity during bending. Additionally, for Fig. 4g, which demonstrates the integration of electronic skin onto a robotic hand, please provide the circuit design diagram and physical images of the data acquisition system used in this setup.
Other suggestions:
1) Several data points in the table in the supplementary information are incorrect. Moreover, the authors compared device parameters under several different light intensity ranges, yet data for their device are missing in multiple segments.
2) It is surprising that the authors even misspelled the abbreviation of their commonly used material, copper phthalocyanine (CuPc).

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors reported the fabrication of the photodetectors based on copper
phthalocyanine/graphene oxide heterojunctions and investigated their photoelectrical
properties. They found that high photoresponsivity can be achieved by enhancing
electronic coupling between photoactive copper phthalocyanine molecules and adjacent
graphene oxide sheets through pressure. The further demonstrated dual-mode electronic
skin application, operable under illumination ranging from daylight to moonlight. Their
study is interesting and useful, supported by rigorous experimental validation,
theoretical modeling, and practical demonstrations. I recommend acceptance pending
revisions to s to address the following technical and conceptual aspects:
We sincerely appreciate the Reviewer’s recognition of the novelty, originality, and
significance of our work, as well as the constructive suggestions. These suggestions
have deepened our mechanistic understanding and helped us to substantially improve
the work. We have conducted additional experiments/analyses and carefully revised the
manuscript accordingly.
1. While the drop-casting method is simple, its reproducibility over larger areas and
feasibility for industrial-scale production should be discussed, along with potential
challenges in uniformity and yield.
Reply: We thank the Reviewer for this very helpful suggestion. In accordance with the
Reviewer’s suggestions, we designed cross-batch validation experiments spanning
multiple production batches. By fabricating a CuPc@GO film with area (3 × 3 cm²), 9
times larger than the original film (1 × 1 cm²) and cutting it into 9 freestanding films,
we encapsulated them in a device with pressure of 240 kPa to fabricate CuPc@GO
photodetectors and test their performance. A total of three batches were prepared, with
each batch taking ten days to complete, and all three batches were finished within one
month. All tested CuPc@GO photodetectors demonstrate stabilized photoresponsivity
(R) values around 1.32 × 10⁷ A/W with variations less than 4.1% (Figs. R1&R2). The
high degree of consistency across different production batches not only demonstrated
the reproducibility but also served as a key indicator for assessing the processing
scalability. The reproducibility experiments, together with ease and high-yield of the
processing of CuPc@GO membranes, confirm the basis for scalable manufacturing and
large-scale productions.

We also fully recognize that progress towards practical applications necessitates
scalability considerations for large-scale fabrication. At the material preparation level,
both CuPc and GO exhibit excellent solution processability. This implies that uniform
CuPc@GO composite films can be continuously and efficiently fabricated on flexible
or rigid substrates via low-cost roll-to-roll coating or large-area inkjet printing
techniques. This non-vacuum, low-temperature process offers significant advantages
over traditional vacuum deposition techniques in terms of equipment investment and
energy consumption. Additionally, at the device integration level, the simple planar
device structure we employ can be combined with established photolithography or
screen-printing electrode patterning processes. This enables the parallel fabrication of
large-scale photodetector arrays, meeting the demands of imaging or sensing
applications.

using the same dip-coating method as that for the CuPc@GO composite film, and spin-

Pure GO does not possess photoelectric activity. We also fabricated GO-only devices
using the same fabrication protocol and measured their photocurrent responses before
and after pressure application (Fig. R5). The GO-only devices exhibited no detectable
photoresponse—pressure application merely enhanced their electrical conductivity.
Consistent with the design rationale of our system, the sandwich structure formed by
the self-assembly of CuPc and GO enables atomic-level interfacial optimization, which
35
is responsible for the significant enhancement of the photoresponse. In the CuPc@GO
photodetector, for the CuPc who is a typical organic photoactive molecule, light
adsorption leads in the formation of an electrically neutral, spatially localized electron-
hole pair. Exciton dissociation requires a donor‒acceptor heterojunction which provides
the interfacial energy offsets to facilitate the generation of free electron and hole.
The CuPc molecule acts as the electron-donor at the heterojunction interface, and GO is
chosen as the electron-acceptor materials owing to their strong electron-accepting
abilities and exceptional flexibility, enabling superior compatibility with small CuPc
molecules and significantly enhancing the number of π-π stacking interactions.
Consequently, once pressure-optimised, a “compact” CuPc-GO heterojunction forms,
establishing sufficient vertical GO-CuPc-GO transport pathways to achieve highly
efficient free carrier transport. It is precisely this sandwich structure that underpins our
outstanding optoelectronic performance.
Our photodetector adopts a vertical structure, employing a design where the CuPc@GO
photoactive layer is sandwiched between top and bottom electrodes, with charge
transport occurring perpendicular to the active layer. In contrast, lateral devices utilise
a three-electrode system comprising two electrodes positioned on either side of the
device and a third electrode for controlling electric field distribution, where carriers rely
on channel transport. Consequently, the photodetector we have fabricated differs from
lateral devices. We are grateful for the Reviewer’s suggestions. Given the complex
equipment requirements and operational mechanisms of lateral devices, we are
considering applying our system to the study of lateral devices. This may form part of
our future research agenda. We appreciate the valuable input of the Reviewer.

d) In Fig. 1d, why does the photoresponsivity reported in the latest literature appear
lower than in earlier studies? Has the performance in this field been deteriorating?
Reply: Regarding Fig. 1d, the apparent decrease in photoresponsivity reported in recent
literature compared to earlier studies is indeed a noteworthy observation. We have also
noted this trend, though the underlying reasons do not appear to be fully understood.
Exploring this phenomenon served as one of the motivations for the present work, as
we suspected that certain factors might have been overlooked.
Based on extensive literature research, the reasons may include the following: the
processing technology of photodetectors has progressed tremendously owing to
advances in material science and device engineering in the past two decades. Many
conventional performance parameters have approached their practical limits.
Consequently, many of the researches have shifted their focus toward developing
materials and devices with distinctive and/or integrated functionalities, such as
flexibility, color sensitivity, biosafety, ultrafast response, and ultrahigh specific
38
detectivity (D*).
Our group have worked on interfacial physics over two decades. We understand that
the manipulation of interfacial behaviour is important to improve the device
performance. For the photodetector, the heterojunction at the donor‒acceptor interface
plays a key role in both charge separation and transport. However, improving the
heterojunction performance usually requires the effective manipulation of
connections/interactions at the heterojunction interface on the atomic scale, which is
highly difficult.
We realized that: i) both the GO sheet and the CuPc molecule have an atomically planar
structure, which facilitates the stress transfer across the heterojunction interface when
external pressure is applied; ii) the GO sheet exhibits mechanical flexibility, enabling
local deformation in response to applied mechanical stimulus; iii) Due to the small size
and non-bonded interactions with GO sheets, CuPc molecules can be repositioned to
better conform to confined spaces, thereby enhancing π‒π stacking interactions under
mechanical stimulation. These characteristics enables easy manipulation of the atomic
interface of the CuPc‒GO heterojunction by a macroscopic stimulation (i.e., an external
force). With the synergy between the unique properties of the CuPc@GO membrane in
the photodetector we fabricated and a modest external pressure (~1 atm), we obtain a
huge improvement in the photoresponsivity (105 to 106-fold).
We think that the strategy we presented here provides a new perspective for fabricating
next-generation photodetectors.

For the UPS experiment, the sample of ∼1 μm thickness CuPc@GO film was first

F
CuPc@GO film was determined to be 4.43 eV.
For pressure-dependent measurements, the sample was first pressurized, then
depressurized, and transferred to the instrument for equivalent vacuum treatment prior
to ex situ measurements. Upon this process, a 0.3 eV shift in the valence band position
of CuPc@GO was observed. Due to its amorphous nature, this system lacks a strictly
defined valence band top, and substantial tail states are expected to be present. The
observed UPS shift is likely due to changes in the band-tail states near the valence band
edge. This 0.3 eV shift under pressure can be attributed to the enhanced electronic
coupling between CuPc and GO. These UPS results (Fig. R12) show that pressurization
strengthens the electronic coupling within the system, thereby facilitating electronic
transports. It is noteworthy that the encapsulated high-pressure apparatus (e.g.,
polyimide-based substrates) cannot be accommodated within the UPS analysis chamber,
thereby rendering in situ characterization unfeasible. Additionally, when these thin
samples undergo off-site measurements after pressurisation, they do not fully revert to
their 1-micrometre thickness state during vacuum extraction, thereby retaining partial
pressure-induced effects.
We note that the conventional method to retrieve the energy band diagram, i.e., using
the UPS results to derive VBM and UV-Vis spectrometer to derive the band gap, is not
suitable for our doped materials. This is mainly because the Tauc plot method [Nat.
Commun. 11, 2304 (2020); Science 358, 1192 (2017) and Nat. Commun. 13, 5216
(2022)] employed for bandgap analysis, utilizing multiple idealized assumptions, is
only applicable to homogeneous bulk materials. Here the CuPc@GO membrane is an
atomic sandwiched structure with complex internal interactions. Therefore, the
proposed results, i.e., the bandgap shift for the CuPc-doped GO and the VBM shift for
the pressurized CuPc@GO, only show some qualitative changes other than the major
feature of GO. Further investigation into the band structure of the CuPc@GO is
precluded by its complicated doped structure.

We have calculated the intra-sheet and inter-sheet electric conductivity of CuPc@GO,
as is shown in Fig. R15. Clearly, even in the presence of the oxidized sites, the GO sheet
exhibits a not-too-low electric intra-sheet conductivity. Under pressure optimization,
the inter-sheet electric conductivity is enhanced by several orders of magnitude, while
the intra-sheet conductivity changes negligibly. The inter-sheet conductivity is still
lower than the intra-sheet conductivity even after the optimization, indicating that the
inter-sheet transport still represents the main bottleneck limiting electron transport in
the overall GO‒CuPc‒GO pathway.
We computed the electrical conductivity σ by using the Boltzmann transport equation
within the constant relaxation time approximation. Consequently, the direct output of
our calculation is the ratio σ/τ , which represents the ideal conductivity governed solely
0
by the material band structure. It is difficult for DFT calculations to evaluate the real
values of the relaxation time τ , which encompasses all scattering processes (e.g.,
0
electron-phonon, impurity, and defect scattering). Additionally, it is also challenging to
perform thorough investigations of excited electron transport by means of time-
dependent density function theory combined with non-adiabatic molecular dynamics.
Given these limitations, the ground-state DFT calculations employed in our study
represent a balanced alternative for describing charge transport properties.

contains five headstages, a microcontroller (MCU, STM32F103, STMicroelectronics,

condition circuit. An operational amplifier (OPA) in the headstage works as a follower
to apply the voltage bias. The acquired data is transmitted by the Bluetooth module
through serial communication. A host computer receives and records the data by using
a custom-designed MATLAB program. To ensure the accuracy of the output voltage
and the acquired data, both the ADC and DAC refer to a high precise voltage reference

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Photodetectors with high photoresponsivity are crucial in a wide range of emerging fields.
Here, we report the realization of photodetectors based on co-assembled composite
membranes consisting of copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) molecules and graphene oxide (GO)
sheets, showing a photoresponsivity as high as ~10⁷ A/W under 3 nW illumination and a
moderate external pressure (~1 atm) in the visible range. We attribute the high
photoresponsivity to the pressure-induced optimization of the atomic-level heterojunctions
between photoactive CuPc molecules and adjacent GO sheets in the photodetector, which
enhances the electronic coupling at the heterojunction for charge transport. The
photodetectors show good flexibility for electronic skin applications, enabling simultaneous
contact sensing and non-contact perception under ambient illumination down to dim
moonlight. The developed strategy provides a promising perspective for fabricating next-
generation photoelectric conversion devices with potential applications spanning intelligent
sensing, aerospace technologies, and defence-related photonic platforms.

---

## Introduction

Photodetectors that convert light into electrical signals are essential for diverse advancing
technologies, such as living cell and biomedical imaging, optical communication, night vision, and
security systems1-5. High photoresponsivity (the responsivity of the photodetector), i.e., the ratio
of the net photocurrent to the incident-light power, is of great importance in practical applications.
Intensive efforts and significant achievements have been made6-16; however, there is only little
progress on the raising of photoresponsivity under the common range of illumination powers (3
nW ‒ 10 mW) in the past decade (Fig. 1d), thus calling for new innovative strategy.

In optoelectronic devices, particularly those based on organics, photoactive materials absorb light
to produce excitons (coupled electrons and holes), and the electrons/holes resulting from the
dissociated excitons transport to the respective acceptor material through a heterojunction17-20. The
performance of the heterojunction is crucial for the photoresponsivity21-24. However, unfavourable
factors, such as defects and unevenness in the photoactive and/or acceptor materials, can degrade
the electronic coupling at the heterojunction for charge separation and transport16,25-27. Clearly,
these unfavourable factors are at the atomic/molecular level, making it very challenging to reduce
the detrimental effects. Fortunately, for materials with a planar architecture, a macroscopic
manipulation (i.e., applying an external pressure) can drive atomic/molecular-level modifications.
Based on our previous works on graphene oxide (GO)28-30, we recently fabricated a composite
membrane consisting of planar structures of copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) molecules and GO
sheets, where CuPc and GO serve as typical photoactive and electron-acceptor materials,
respectively31. We expected that a simple macroscopic manipulation could reduce some
detrimental effects to make a more compact CuPc‒GO heterojunction, thus leading to an even
higher photoresponsivity.

Electronic skins (e-skins) hold great transformative potentials32,33. Current e-skin technologies
predominantly rely on contact-based sensing modalities to acquire environmental information34,35.
Although this mode is effective for static scenarios, it fails to address dynamic environments
requiring non-contact interactions, such as robot-assisted navigation or preemptive hazard
detection in vehicular safety systems. Conventional optical e-skins, employing radar, laser, or
infrared light, require additional active illumination, and face critical limitations under passive
natural light conditions36. Clearly, if there is an ultrasensitive photodetector to detect direction and
distance, as well as flexibility and piezoelectricity to monitor the subjected pressure, we can obtain
a dual-mode e-skin simultaneously realizing contact and non-contact sensing under ambient
illumination.

Here, we present a photodetector based on a co-assembled composite membrane consisting of
CuPc molecules and GO sheets (CuPc@GO), exhibiting high responsivity under 3 nW ‒ 10 mW
incident powers and moderate external pressure within the near-ultraviolet, visible and infrared
bands. We associate the high photoresponsivity to the optimization of the atomic-level CuPc‒GO
heterojunctions via a macroscopic manipulation ‒ by simply applying a modest external pressure
(~1 atm), a strong electronic coupling at the heterojunction is established and a ~105 to 106-fold
improvement in photoresponsivity is obtained. The photodetector is successfully used in dual-
mode e-skins, enabling flexibility together with simultaneous contact and non-contact sensing,
within the irradiation range from daylight to moonlight.

---

## Results

High photoresponsivity obtained under external pressure

The central component of the photodetector is a CuPc@GO membrane fabricated via a drop
casting method. Briefly, a CuPc suspension was mixed with a GO dispersion. The mixture was
then dripped onto release paper and dried, yielding a composite membrane. The membrane was
subsequently employed to fabricate a CuPc@GO photodetector.

To ensure that the embedded CuPc molecules contact the GO sheets well, we applied an external
force (i.e., pressure) on the CuPc@GO membrane. Henceforth, we refer to the CuPc@GO
membranes with and without the pressure as optimized and unoptimized membranes, respectively.
Simultaneously, we illuminated the optimized CuPc@GO membrane with a beam of light on the
opposite side from the pressure application site, with the illuminated area of 1 cm2 identical to the
area under external pressure (Fig. 1a). In this paper, the illumination wavelength is 635 nm (visible
light) unless otherwise explicitly stated. The current‒voltage (I‒V) performance with an incident
power E = 3 nW was examined firstly (Fig. 1b). As the bias ranges from -1.2 to 1.2 V, the
in
photocurrent increases with the increasing pressure (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1). When the
external pressure (denoted as P) reaches 240 kPa, the photocurrent increases to 4.41 × 10-2 A under
a bias of 1.2 V, in contrast to the dark current of 4.11 × 10-3 A. Notably, the photocurrent and dark
current in the unoptimized case are only 5.35 × 10-8 A and 1.87 × 10-8 A, respectively. Thus, the
light response is boosted by more than 105 times under P = 240 kPa, while it is only modest in the
absence of the external pressure.

The device works with high photoresponsivity across a broad wavelength range. The values of R

The CuPc@GO detector achieves a lower detection limit of only 100 pW (Fig. 1g) for illumination
power at room temperature without requiring an additional photomultiplier, which reaches the
upper limit of the working range for single-photon detectors39. Moreover, the optimization greatly
raises the response speed of the photodetector – both the rise time (τ) and decay time (τ ) were
r d

microseconds (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 5).

The high photoresponsivity shows strong stability (Supplementary Figs. 6&7) and reproducibility
among different production batches (Supplementary Figs. 8&9), insensitive to ambient humidity
while sensitive to the oxidation degree of GO (Supplementary Figs. 10&11).

Characterization of CuPc@GO membrane under pressure

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern (Fig. 2a) indicates an intersheet spacing of 0.826 nm for the
unoptimized CuPc@GO membrane, which is slightly larger than that for the pure GO membrane
(0.731 nm). This suggests that the CuPc molecules, which have a planar structure and single-atom
thickness, intercalate into the GO membrane and form a single-molecule layer sandwiched
between two adjacent GO sheets. The intercalation of CuPc is also supported by scanning electron
microscopy (SEM), where a well-defined layered structure (Fig. 2b) of the CuPc@GO membrane
(unoptimized) was clearly revealed. Compared with the pure GO membrane, a new sharp
diffraction peak in the XRD pattern (Fig. 2a) appears at ~26° for the CuPc@GO membrane,
corresponding to an interplanar spacing of ~0.334 nm, indicating the stacking of CuPc aromatic
rings with the unoxidized regions40,41 of the GO sheets.

The XRD patterns after the pressure application are shown in Fig. 2a. Notably, as the pressure
increases, the intersheet spacing of the composite membrane decreases continuously (Fig. 2c), and
the peak at ~26° corresponding to an interplanar spacing of 0.334 nm becomes more apparent.
These phenomena indicate that the confined space between the GO sheets is gradually regulated
such that more π‒π stacks are enabled between the aromatic rings of the CuPc molecules and the
GO sheets.

We further performed femtosecond transient absorption (TA)42 spectroscopy measurements (with
an external pressure ~25 kPa; see Methods). The TA spectra of the optimized (Fig. 2d) and
unoptimized (Supplementary Fig. 12) membranes pumped by a 400 nm laser pulse show clear
excited-state absorbance (ESA) signals peaking at ~650 nm, whereas ground-state bleaching (GSB)
and stimulated emission (SE) signals are not observed. The ESA signals span a broad range of
wavelengths, from ~550 nm to 800 nm (and beyond), and exhibit a large overlap with the typical
absorption spectrum of the CuPc molecule (Supplementary Fig. 13), indicating that the
photocurrent is mainly caused by the optical absorption of CuPc molecules. The absence of GSB
and SE signals can be attributed to aggregation-induced quenching43 of excitons in CuPc molecules
because of their strong π‒π stacking with neighbouring GO sheets, which leads to ultrafast charge
dynamics and is beneficial to the high photoresponsivity.

Multiexponential fitting with time constants of τ , τ , and τ was applied to the TA kinetics data

(Fig. 2e). The same abrupt increase in the ESA signal (with a time scale of ~ 0.9 ps) can be observed
for both the optimized and unoptimized CuPc@GO membranes, implying the immediate
generation of charge carriers right after the application of the laser pump. Then, two different
charge dynamics processes can be identified: i) the ultrafast transfer of the charge carrier from the
CuPc molecules to the neighbouring GO sheets, of which the characteristic time τ is reduced from
1

and inter-sheet charge transport (bridged by the CuPc molecule), of which the characteristic time
τ is reduced from 4.33 ps to 2.56 ps. Another possible process involved in the TA kinetics is the
2

sheets, of which a much larger characteristic time τ (~15‒16 ps) is almost independent of the
3
pressure.

Mechanism of the pressure-enhanced photoresponsivity

To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we performed density functional theory (DFT)
calculations on the unit cell of the composite membrane ‒ a sandwich complex where one CuPc
molecule is placed between adjacent GO sheets. Here we used a simplified GO model44: one
epoxide group and one hydroxy group were located closely to each other and separately on both
sides of the GO sheet, leaving a relatively large region unoxidized. This model is consistent with
previous reports that the oxidized groups tend to gather and there are large unoxidized regions on
the GO sheets40,41. Considering the observation of remarkable π‒π stacking interactions between
the CuPc molecules and the GO sheets (Fig. 2b,c), the CuPc molecule was placed in the middle of
the unoxidized regions of the GO sheets. Two typical states were considered: the coupling state
and the uncoupling state, corresponding to the cases of small and large intersheet distance,
respectively (see Fig. 3a,b). In the coupling state, a CuPc molecule has an equal distance of 0.327
nm with each GO sheet, yielding the intersheet distance of 0.654 nm according to structural
optimization (Fig. 3a). The coupling state corresponds to the pressure-optimized configuration.

The well-dispersed valence and conduction bands (Fig. 3c) and the delocalized electronic
wavefunction distribution (Fig. 3a) clearly indicate strong electronic coupling at the CuPc‒GO
interface. Consequently, a charge-transport channel is well formed perpendicular to the GO sheets,
which is bridged by the CuPc molecule. The valence and conduction bandwidths are 13.8 meV
and 8.2 meV, respectively, which corresponds to a coupling at the CuPc‒GO interface of 3.5 meV
for the hole and 2.1 meV for the electron according to the one-dimensional tight-binding model.
This result is consistent with our ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) data, which show
a shift in the valence band position due to pressure optimization (Supplementary Fig. 14). In
addition, we calculated the intra-sheet and inter-sheet electric conductivities to quantitively
characterize the relative contributions of intra- and inter-sheets to charge transport as well as the
influence of pressure (see Supplementary Fig. 15). The inter-sheet conductivity is still lower than
the intra-sheet conductivity even after the optimization, indicating that the inter-sheet transport
still represents the main bottleneck limiting charge transport in the overall GO‒CuPc‒GO pathway.

In the typical uncoupling state, the intersheet distance was set to be 0.826 nm, corresponding to
the intersheet spacing of the unoptimized CuPc@GO membrane (see Fig. 2b). The valence and
conduction bandwidths are sharply reduced to 0.9 meV and 1.6 meV, respectively. We also show
the case of pure GO system (parallel GO sheets without CuPc) as the control group in Fig. 3c,
where the bandwidths are also negligible due to the absence of intersheet interactions. These results
indicate negligible electronic coupling in the uncoupling case, as also demonstrated by the much
more localized electronic wavefunction distribution along the perpendicular direction (Fig. 3b).
Now we can illustrate how efficient charge-transport pathways are established in the CuPc@GO
membrane and why the applied pressure serves as a key. As shown in Fig. 3d, the CuPc molecules
are distributed between the GO sheets. There are two processes associated with the transport of
charge carriers: (i) the electron transfer from the CuPc molecule onto the neighbouring GO sheet
due to exciton dissociation; and (ii) the intra-sheet and inter-sheet (via a GO‒CuPc‒GO pathway)
charge transport. In the absence of the external pressure, due to the relatively large distance
between CuPc and GO sheets, there are rare coupling states to form efficient pathways for charge
transfer and intersheet charge transport (Fig. 3e). However, through the application of pressure,
most hindrance mentioned above are removed and much more coupling states with efficient
charge-transport pathways are well established (Fig. 3d), thus resulting in a high photocurrent.

Dual-mode-sensing electronic skin of the photodetector

We fabricated a CuPc@GO-based electronic skin (CuPc@GO e-skin) which can work in both non-
contact and contact sensing modes (Fig. 4a). We note that the CuPc@GO photodetector has good
flexibility with high photoresponsivity remaining at various bending/twisting angles (Fig. 4b and
Supplementary Figs. A16&17). Thus, the photodetector can have more applications requiring
flexibility45 such as the e-skin. Standard models with sizes of ~10 cm were used to testify the dual-
mode sensing under ambient illumination with E = 10 μW, corresponding to the ambient
in
illumination just at dawn (~9.5 lux for the CuPc@GO membrane with an area of 1 × 1 cm2). As e-
skin approaches the models, the photocurrents decrease commenced at the distances of 15 mm, 12
mm, and 5 mm, for cuboid, hemisphere and stick, respectively, exhibiting dependence on both
object geometry and separation distance (Fig. 4c). Once the e-skin contacts the models, an abrupt
current increase is observed (Fig. 4c), which also exhibits a shape-dependent manner mainly due
to the piezoelectricity of the CuPc@GO membrane (see Ref. 31 and Supplementary Table 2). The
e-skin can also distinguish the hardness of objects ‒ an object with higher hardness can induce a
more abrupt current increase as the e-skin contacts the object (Fig. 4d). As the target size increases,
the e-skin shows an extended range of object discrimination, enabling non-contact detection at
distances up to 2 m for the target with a size of ~1 m (Fig. 4e). Remarkably, the e-skin can “see”
the object even under a power of 900 pW (Fig. 4f), corresponding to the ambient illumination
under the moonlight (~0.01 Lux for the CuPc@GO membrane).

We designed a control board for signal acquisition and actuation of the robotic manipulator (Fig.
4g and Supplementary Fig. 18), which was subsequently installed on a robotic manipulator
incorporating the CuPc@GO e-skin into the fingertips (Fig. 4h). A series of actions including
approaching, grasping, moving and releasing were conducted by using the robotic manipulator
according to the e-skin feedback, and the featured responses in the photocurrent are explicated in
Fig. 4i, with the middle fingertip as a typical example to illustrate the idea (Fig. 4j). Firstly, the
middle finger was controlled to approach the target object, inducing a decreasing photocurrent.
According to the results of standard models, a 1.9% reduction in the photocurrent serves as a
threshold for impending mechanical contact. Once the current decreased lower than this threshold,
the approaching velocity was initially halved and then progressively attenuated to 0.9 mm/s,
thereby minimizing impulse transfer to the object. The manipulating examples with a banana (Fig.
4i,j) and an egg (Supplementary Fig. 19) the successfully touching on the objects while avoiding
damage. During the releasing process, all fingers retract simultaneously, exhibiting fast decreases
in the current (Fig. 4i,j and Supplementary Fig. 19).

---

## Methods

Materials

The Copper phthalocyanine and Graphite were provided by Aladdin Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China)
with a purity beyond 99.95%. Potassium persulfate (K S O ), Phosphorus pentoxide (P O ),
2 2 8 2 5
Sulfuric acid (H SO ), Potassium permanganate (KMnO ) and Hydrogen peroxide (H O ) were
2 4 4 2 2
purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. All reagents were used as received. Milli-
Q water (18.25 MΩ, Millipore, US) was used to prepare GO aqueous dispersions. The
programmable robotic manipulator (uHand 2.0) was provided by Hiwonder Tech Co., Ltd.
(Shenzhen, China).

Preparation of CuPc@GO composite membranes and photodetectors

A GO suspension (5 mg/mL) was prepared with GO synthesized from natural graphite powder
using an improved Hummers method. A CuPc suspension was prepared by adding 28.68 mg of
powder to a centrifuge tube containing 50 mL of water, followed by an ultrasonic treatment for 1
hour. The CuPc dispersion was thoroughly mixed with the 5 mg/mL GO dispersion in equal
volumes. Ultrapure water of the same volume was subsequently added, and the resulting mixture
was processed with ultrasonic treatment for 1 hour to yield a stable CuPc@GO suspension. The
composite suspension was then divided into equal-volume droplets, which were dripped onto
release paper for self-assembly and dried in an oven at 70℃ for 12 hours. This process resulted in
the formation of the CuPc@GO composite membrane which has a thickness of ~1 μm with good
flexibility. Next, the membrane was peeled off from the release paper and then trimmed into square
pieces measuring 1 × 1 cm2. The CuPc@GO membrane within this photodetector served as the
photon-sensing layer.

Measurement of the photodetector properties

The I‒V characteristics and photocurrent versus time curves of the photodetectors were measured
using a Keithley 2461 source meter (Tektronix, USA) following rigorous experimental procedures.
To ensure accurate signal transmission and to minimize external interference, a gold probe was
employed during the photocurrent measurements. The external pressure was applied by the weight
unless otherwise explicated stated and was calibrated with commercial pressure transducers. The
incident light sources were monochromatic lasers (Thorlabs, USA) with an adjustable power
density and were precisely calibrated with photodiode power detectors (Thorlabs, S170C and
PM100D, USA) with 10 nW detection limit. The 3-nW incident power was achieved by attenuating
the 10 nW source through a neutral density filter with 30% transmittance. The illumination position
and area (1 cm2) were kept consistent throughout all the measurements, except for the case of 100
pW incident power which was achieved by reducing the effective optical area of the device to 0.1
× 0.1 cm² via a mask. Notably, no light source other than the laser was present in the measured
environment. Moreover, the photodetectors were tested under conditions consisting of room
temperature (25°C), 20% humidity, and atmospheric pressure. The rise and decay times were
obtained using an oscilloscope (Tektronix, MSO44 4-BW-200).

Characterization of the CuPc@GO membranes

Lateral images of the CuPc@GO membranes were acquired via secondary electron imaging in the
scanning electron microscope (ZEISS Gemini 300, Germany) at an accelerating voltage of 3 kV.
Patterns of X-ray diffraction were obtained via XRD (Rigaku Ultimate IV, Japan) with a Cu Kα
radiation source (λ = 0.15418 nm) in the 2θ range of 5°~40°. Before the XRD experiments were
conducted, pressures with different values (ranging from 20 to 240 kPa) were applied to the
CuPc@GO membrane for 5 minutes. There is no pressure applied on the sample during the XRD
experiments.

Transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy

Femtosecond TA spectroscopy was carried out using a Helios ultrafast pump‒probe system, which
included an oscillator and a Coherent Opera Solo optical parametric amplifier. The titanium
sapphire amplifier in the system generates 800 nm pulses at a repetition rate of 1 kHz, with each
pulse having a duration of 70 fs. These pulses are split by a beam splitter: one portion is directed
to a TOPAS parametric amplifier (Coherent) to produce the pump pulses while the other is focused
onto sapphire and YAG plates, generating a white supercontinuum that covers the 420–780 nm and
800–1400 nm ranges, respectively. The time delay between the pump and probe pulses has a
maximum value of 8 ns when a motorized optical delay line is used.

In order to meet the requirements of the TA spectroscopy measurement, both the membrane
thickness and the pressure applied are different from those of other experiments: i) the TA
measurement requires the sample surface to be very flat, so the CuPc@GO suspension was
carefully deposited via the drop-casting technique onto a 2 cm × 2 cm high-clarity quartz glass
substrate, followed by drying in an oven at 70°C. This results in a membrane thickness of ~ 100
nm, much thinner than that in other experiments (~1 μm). ii) Considering the fragility of the glass,
we applied a small pressure of ~25 kPa on the sample for 5 minutes. During the TA spectroscopy
measurements, the pressure was removed.

Dual-mode sensing of the electronic skin

The flexible CuPc@GO photodetector was mounted at the fingertip of a robotic manipulator to
maintain its optimal operational state during photodetection. For non-contact sensing, the robotic
system drove the fingertip in a programmed, controlled trajectory, advancing it toward the target
object until the initial surface contact was established. After contact, the system applied a
controlled compressive force by advancing the fingertip an additional 1 mm. During the entire
process, the current signals were monitored in real-time. Dynamic analysis on the current variation
enables the real-time capture of the mechanical interaction state between the fingertip and the
object, facilitating closed-loop feedback for precise adjustment of the motion trajectory of the
manipulator. This adaptive strategy ensures both accuracy and efficiency in the process of object
grasping. Environmental illumination remained stable throughout all experimental procedures.

Theoretical calculations

DFT calculations were performed with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)46.
Projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials were applied. The generalized gradient
approximation (GGA) of the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) formalism was used to treat the
exchange‒correlation interaction between electrons47, and the DFT-D3 method of Grimme with a
zero-damping function48 was applied for dispersion correction. The electron wavefunction was
expanded on a plane-wave basis set with an energy cutoff of 450 eV. The Brillouin zones were
sampled by k-point grids of 2 × 2 × 3 for structural optimization49.

For structural optimization of the state without an external pressure, the periodicity along the
direction perpendicular to the GO sheets was set to 0.826 nm, consistent with the XRD result,
whereas those along the other two directions were calculated to fully relax the stress. To describe
the state with an external pressure, the restriction of the periodicity along the z-axis was released,
and the structure was reoptimized via DFT calculations, resulting in a new periodicity of 0.654 nm,
which represents the deformation influenced by the external pressure. After the entire structural
optimization process, the number of k-points in the Brillouin zone was increased, and non-self-
consistent calculations were performed to obtain the energy band. By using the one-dimensional
tight-binding model, the intersheet electronic coupling 𝑡 for electrons/holes was then
